Doing so, and online optimization of reconstruction parameters, and/or creation of ‘meta-algorithms’ that either alert users of how best to analyze generated data or reconfigure parameters automatically are all technology development opportunities that would benefit any application that would couple SDF with imaging modalities. 2.3.4 Volumetric Imaging Volumetric imaging capabilities that are coupled with SDF would have numerous applications within civil nuclear power, hold-up quantification, and ER. Presently, volumetric imaging is rarely done outside of research settings due to the need to manually align measurements and maps and the need to make assumptions concerning attenuation. As SDF is loosely akin to free-moving computed tomography (CT), mathematically, volumetric imaging would be akin to SPECT-CT wherein CT image is created of a patient in order to correct for the attenuation of the emitted γ rays during a single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) assay. Coupling SDF measurements with semantic labels could automatically provide algorithms with attenuation priors, helping develop both attenuation-aware search algorithms and hold-up quantification with bounded uncertainties. Further coupling of SDF with precise attenuation estimates either from design files, radiography, CT, or back-scatter imaging would allow SDF algorithms to achieve volumetric imaging accuracy that would dramatically outpace other passive volumetric imaging capabilities. Volumetric SDF imaging was actually demonstrated at nearly the same time as the now more mature surface activity mapping [48]. There are three technical reasons that volumetric mapping was not pursued as actively as surface mapping. First, performing SDF analyses on volumes is more computationally expensive.
